passage.title: The Power of Giving Ground
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Clara tapped her stack of blue index cards against the wood podium in the school library. As captain of the fifth-grade debate team, she had spent two weeks getting ready for this match. Her goal was to argue that the town should trade its old school buses for electric ones. In past matches, Clara treated every debate like a tug-of-war where giving an inch meant losing the whole rope. She thought a strong speaker had to block every single claim from the other side. Across the aisle, Marcus adjusted his glasses and spread out a neat chart of town budget numbers.

When the timekeeper rang the small brass bell, Clara stepped up to the microphone and read her opening speech. During the opening round on the stage, her best point about solar roof panels was quickly challenged by a sharp question from the opposing captain. Marcus pointed out that electric buses cost nearly twice as much to buy upfront as regular buses. He warned the three judges that a small town would have to cut park repairs just to pay for the new fleet.

Back at her table during the two-minute break, Clara reached for a red card. That card brushed off starting costs as a small detail. Yet when she looked at the judges' faces, she saw them nodding at Marcus's budget chart. If she acted stubborn and pretended the high price tag did not matter, the judges would stop trusting her numbers. Her coach had once told her that admitting a real drawback makes the rest of a speaker's plan sound much more honest.

Clara set the red card aside and wrote two fresh lines on a blank white card. When the bell rang for her next turn, she looked straight at Marcus and smiled. She chose to concede that buying electric buses costs more in the first year, and she agreed that the town should not buy twenty new buses at once. Then she pivoted to her fuel and repair chart. Buying just two new buses each year when old ones wore out would save huge sums on fuel. By year four, those savings would pay for the next bus.

Marcus blinked in surprise. He had prepared to fight an all-or-nothing plan, not a slow step-by-step swap. By admitting the high starting price, Clara made her long-term savings plan look fair and credible to the panel. When the head judge named the winner, she praised Clara for using the other side's worry to build a smart plan. Clara shook Marcus's hand, knowing that true strength in a debate can start with giving ground.

tier2Words.definition: refusing to change one's mind or course of action despite good reasons to do so
tier2Words.rootHint: Middle English 'stoburn' (untamable or fixed like a tree stump)
tier2Words.contextClue: Clara realized she should not refuse to budge and pretend the high price tag did not matter.

tier2Words.definition: to admit that a point is true or valid after first resisting it
tier2Words.contextClue: Clara admitted that buying electric buses costs more in the first year instead of denying Marcus's point.

tier2Words.definition: turned or shifted smoothly to a new point or direction
tier2Words.rootHint: French 'pivot' (a central pin on which something turns)
tier2Words.contextClue: After agreeing about first-year costs, Clara shifted the focus to her fuel and repair savings chart.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"During the opening round on the stage, her best point about solar roof panels was quickly challenged by a sharp question from the opposing captain."

Based on the structure of this sentence, what actually challenged Clara's point?

options.text: A sharp question from the opposing captain
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'was quickly challenged by' tells us that 'a sharp question from the opposing captain' is what challenged Clara's point about solar roof panels.

options.text: The solar roof panels on the school buses
options.childFeedback: 'About solar roof panels' only describes what Clara's point was about—the solar panels didn't ask a question or challenge her speech!

options.text: The opening round clock on the library stage
options.childFeedback: 'During the opening round on the stage' tells when and where Clara spoke, not what challenged her point.

options.text: The timekeeper ringing the small brass bell
options.childFeedback: The timekeeper only rang the small brass bell to start the round in Paragraph 2; it was the opposing captain's sharp question that challenged Clara.

questions.provingSentenceText: During the opening round on the stage, her best point about solar roof panels was quickly challenged by a sharp question from the opposing captain.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'was quickly challenged by' tells us that 'a sharp question from the opposing captain' is what challenged Clara's point about solar roof panels.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'her best point about solar roof panels' receives the action. The true actor performing 'was challenged' comes after 'by': 'a sharp question from the opposing captain' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look right after 'was quickly challenged by' in Paragraph 2 to see what actually challenged Clara's point.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"She chose to concede that buying electric buses costs more in the first year, and she agreed that the town should not buy twenty new buses at once."

What does the word "concede" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: To shout loudly so the judges cannot hear the other team
options.childFeedback: Clara doesn't shout over Marcus; in Paragraph 4, she looks at him, smiles calmly, and admits his point about first-year bus costs is true.

options.text: To admit that an opponent's point is true
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'concede' means to admit that an opponent's point is true. Right after 'concede,' the sentence gives the clue 'and she agreed,' and Paragraph 5 says 'By admitting the high starting price.'

options.text: To hide a stack of index cards inside a desk drawer
options.childFeedback: Clara sets her red card aside on the table in Paragraph 4, but 'concede' refers to what she says at the microphone: admitting that electric buses cost more upfront.

options.text: To prove that an opponent's math chart is completely fake
options.childFeedback: Trying to prove Marcus's chart fake is the opposite of 'concede'! Clara realizes the judges trust his budget chart, so she admits his upfront cost point is right.

questions.provingSentenceText: She chose to concede that buying electric buses costs more in the first year, and she agreed that the town should not buy twenty new buses at once.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'concede' means to admit that an opponent's point is true. Right after 'concede,' the sentence gives the clue 'and she agreed,' and Paragraph 5 says 'By admitting the high starting price.'
questions.parentExplanation: The parallel phrase 'and she agreed' in Paragraph 4, along with Paragraph 5's 'By admitting the high starting price,' confirms that 'concede' means to admit that an opponent's point is true (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at the second half of the sentence in Paragraph 4 ('and she agreed') and the start of Paragraph 5 ('By admitting') for context clues.

questions.prompt: Why does Clara decide not to use her red index card during the prep break in Paragraph 3?

options.text: She runs out of time before the brass bell rings for the second round.
options.childFeedback: Clara doesn't run out of time during the two-minute break; she sets the red card aside on purpose and writes two fresh lines on a blank white card.

options.text: She notices that the red card has the wrong town name written across the top.
options.childFeedback: Nothing is wrong with the town name on the red card! Paragraph 3 says the red card brushed off starting costs as a small detail, which would look stubborn.

options.text: She sees the judges nodding at Marcus's chart and realizes that brushing off the high cost will make her lose their trust.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Clara sees the judges nodding at Marcus's budget chart and realizes that if she uses the red card to brush off the high upfront cost, the judges will stop trusting her numbers.

options.text: She decides that diesel buses are actually cleaner and cheaper than electric buses.
options.childFeedback: Clara still argues for electric buses in Paragraph 4! She simply switches to a step-by-step plan of buying two electric buses each year.

questions.provingSentenceText: If she acted stubborn and pretended the high price tag did not matter, the judges would stop trusting her numbers.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, Clara sees the judges nodding at Marcus's budget chart and realizes that if she uses the red card to brush off the high upfront cost, the judges will stop trusting her numbers.

questions.prompt: How does the tug-of-war comparison in Paragraph 1 help the reader understand Clara's change in Paragraph 4?

options.text: It shows that Clara never cared about winning debates until she met Marcus.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 shows the exact opposite: Clara was the debate team captain and had spent two weeks preparing because she cared deeply about winning!

options.text: It explains why the debate team practices pulling ropes in the school gym before every library match.
options.childFeedback: Nobody is pulling literal ropes in the gym! 'Tug-of-war' is a figure of speech in Paragraph 1 describing how Clara used to argue in debates.

options.text: It proves that Marcus was much stronger than Clara during last year's field day games.
options.childFeedback: The story is about a fifth-grade library debate on school budgets, not a physical field day game between Marcus and Clara.

options.text: It shows how Clara used to think giving an inch meant losing, which contrasts with her winning choice to concede a point later.
options.childFeedback: Comparing debate to a tug-of-war where 'giving an inch meant losing the whole rope' in Paragraph 1 shows how stubborn Clara used to be, making her choice to concede a point in Paragraph 4 a big change.

questions.provingSentenceText: In past matches, Clara treated every debate like a tug-of-war where giving an inch meant losing the whole rope.
questions.childTip: Comparing debate to a tug-of-war where 'giving an inch meant losing the whole rope' in Paragraph 1 shows how stubborn Clara used to be, making her choice to concede a point in Paragraph 4 a big change.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 establishes Clara's initial rigid mindset ('giving an inch meant losing the whole rope'), which highlights her character growth in Paragraph 4 when she yields on upfront cost to win the larger argument (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Compare Clara's old 'tug-of-war' rule in Paragraph 1 with what she learns at the end of Paragraph 5 about 'giving ground.'

questions.prompt: PART A: Why does Clara's revised argument in Paragraph 4 convince the judges to name her the winner?

options.text: By acknowledging the high upfront cost and proposing a gradual two-bus-per-year replacement plan, she makes her savings argument realistic.
options.childFeedback: By admitting that electric buses cost more upfront and proposing a gradual two-bus-per-year swap paid for by fuel savings, Clara makes her plan look realistic, fair, and believable to the judges.

options.text: By proving that electric buses actually cost half as much to buy as standard diesel buses, she shows Marcus made a math error.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says electric buses cost nearly twice as much upfront, and in Paragraph 4 Clara admits that high starting cost is true rather than calling it a math error.

options.text: By promising that students will wash all twenty buses for free every weekend, she saves the town money.
options.childFeedback: Clara never talks about students washing buses on weekends; her savings come from spending less money on fuel and repairs over four years.

options.text: By reading her red index card louder than Marcus spoke, she keeps the judges from looking at his budget chart.
options.childFeedback: Clara set the red card aside in Paragraph 4 and never read it! She won by listening to Marcus's cost concern and building a smarter plan.

questions.provingSentenceText: By admitting the high starting price, Clara made her long-term savings plan look fair and credible to the panel.
questions.childTip: By admitting that electric buses cost more upfront and proposing a gradual two-bus-per-year swap paid for by fuel savings, Clara makes her plan look realistic, fair, and believable to the judges.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RL1, Clara wins over the panel because she admits the high starting price and proposes buying just two buses a year so fuel savings help pay for future buses, making her plan fair and credible (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at Paragraphs 4 and 5 to see how admitting the upfront cost and proposing a two-bus-per-year plan impressed the judges.
